title: Workflows vs agents: who controls the steps

items.stem: What decides whether a system is a fixed workflow rather than an agent?

options.text: Whether a human reviews its output before it is used
Whether the code sets the order, or the model decides live
Whether it calls a language model at any point
How many steps it takes before it finishes

items.stem: Your booking code always checks training, then the calendar, then books the slot; one step calls a model to read the student's request. Is this a workflow or an agent?

options.text: An agent, because it calls a language model
An agent, because it uses more than one tool
Neither, because a workflow can never call a model
A workflow, because the step order is fixed in code

items.stem: Which of these makerspace tasks fits a fixed workflow better than an agent?

options.text: Checking whether a student is trained on one named machine
Recommending which machine best suits a vague project idea
Diagnosing an error message a student pastes in, unseen before
Suggesting print settings for a material no one has tried

items.stem: Your model budget is small. For a simple, repeatable check, why might a workflow beat an agent?

options.text: Agents should never be used, since they always cost more
A workflow cannot call a model, so it is cheaper
It skips the model re-deciding the same step every run
Cost is the same either way, so design does not matter

items.stem: A student asks what resin-print settings would survive boiling water for an odd-shaped part. Is this better answered by a fixed workflow or an agent?
Your assistant currently lets the model decide even whether a slot is still free before confirming a booking. Why would a fixed workflow fit that check better?
